one_liner: Closed-source CUDA add-on to CKTSO for sparse LU refactorization and solve; first-party 13.3x geomean refactorization speedup over KLU.
what_it_does: CKTSO-GPU moves the repeated part of circuit-simulation solving onto an NVIDIA GPU: numeric refactorization with a fixed pivot order, and forward/backward substitution. CKTSO still does analysis and the first factorization with pivoting on the CPU. Then CKTSO_InitializeGpuAccelerator copies CKTSO's LU structure to the GPU, and CKTSO_GpuRefactorize and CKTSO_GpuSolve take new values and right-hand sides from host memory. The C API has five functions plus a C++ interface struct, with 32-bit and 64-bit index variants (_L); it handles real and complex matrices, in row or column mode.
how_it_is_fast: Refactorization reuses the pivot order and LU pattern fixed by the CPU factorization, so there is no pivot search and the column dependencies are known in advance; the GPU can then factor independent columns in parallel. The guide exposes a threshold (iparm[1], default 128) that switches refactorization between a 'bulk' and a 'pipeline' mode, and it picks blocks per multiprocessor and threads per block automatically. This matches the author's published GPU left-looking LU (DAC 2012, TPDS 2015), which uses a cluster mode for early dependency levels with many sparse independent columns and a pipeline mode for late levels with few, denser columns (per search snippets; the source is closed, so the exact algorithm is not visible). Gains come from matrices with enough work per factor nonzero; the guide's threshold is flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50.
when_to_use: SPICE Newton/transient loops that refactor the same circuit-matrix pattern thousands of times while the pivot order from one CPU factorization stays acceptable.
Slightly dense circuit matrices that pass the user guide's flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50 test, the only class it was benchmarked on.
You already use CKTSO on x86-64 Windows or Linux and have an NVIDIA GPU of compute capability 3.5-8.0 with a CUDA 11 driver.
Real or complex matrices with a single right-hand side per solve.
when_not_to_use: Highly sparse circuit matrices: the user guide itself says it cannot accelerate them efficiently and that multicore CKTSO is best there.

You have a many-core CPU: the GPU was compared only with one-thread CKTSO and sequential KLU. The CKTSO README separately claims more than 25x over KLU at 16 threads (66 matrices, a different set), which exceeds this module's 13.29x geomean over KLU, so multithreaded CKTSO may match or beat it (cross-document, not like-for-like).
You need pivoting on the GPU: factorization with pivoting stays on the CPU, and every CPU refactorization that changes the LU structure requires calling InitializeGpuAccelerator again.

You need source code, a license, non-x86-64 hosts, AMD GPUs, or post-Ampere GPUs: it ships only prebuilt x86-64 binaries with no license terms, built with CUDA 11.0, and the listed compute capabilities stop at 8.0.
Long-term support: the last commit was 2023-04-01, and the CKTSO README lists a 'faster GPU acceleration method' as work in progress.

integration.form: shared lib (prebuilt libcktsogpu.so / cktsogpu.dll + .lib, with _l variants for 64-bit indices; header cktso-gpu.h)
integration.dependencies: CKTSO shared library and header plus its cktso.lic file (separate repo; CKTSO 20230325 or later); NVIDIA CUDA 11.0 runtime and driver (Linux 450.51.05, Windows 451.48 or newer)
integration.min_toolchain: Prebuilt with gcc 4.8.5 on CentOS 7 and Visual Studio 2019 on Windows, CUDA 11.0; plain C API usable from C or C++ (demo Makefile uses g++ -O3)
integration.platforms: x86-64 Windows or Linux only; NVIDIA GPUs with compute capability 3.5, 3.7, 5.0, 5.2, 6.0, 6.1, 7.0, 7.5 or 8.0 listed (RTX 3090 used in results); V100 needs the disabledL1cache build

gotchas: Wrong results on some GPUs: disabledL1cache/readme.txt says the V100 needs the L1-cache-disabled libraries, which cost about 20% performance. Check residuals on your GPU.

GpuRefactorize does no pivoting. If changed values make a pivot unacceptable, fall back to CKTSO factorization with pivoting on the CPU and re-initialize the accelerator; CKTSO's scaling option (its iparm[7]) is not supported on the GPU.
Values and vectors are passed in host memory, and results.pdf does not say whether its timings include host-device transfers; oparm[1]/oparm[2] report the module's own timings.

Return codes are mixed: negative values are CKTSO errors (-51 to -53 are GPU-specific), and positive values are raw cudaError_t codes (e.g. 209, no kernel image, on an unsupported GPU). Call CKTSO_SortFactors before initializing, or initialization is slower.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Use it only if you already run CKTSO and your matrices pass the flops/NNZ(L+U) > 50 test. Otherwise multithreaded CKTSO (same author, maintained, TCAD 2025 paper) or BSD-licensed Basker on the CPU is the safer choice, and GLU is a public-source GPU circuit LU you can build and modify.
verified_claims_summary: First-party results.pdf (CKTSO-GPU 20221207), 29 SuiteSparse circuit matrices with Flops/NZ(L+U) > 50: refactorization on an RTX 3090 is 13.29x faster on geometric mean (28.80x arithmetic) than sequential KLU 1.3.9 given CKTSO's ordering, and 6.11x (12.01x) faster than CKTSO on one thread of a Xeon Gold 6130. Solve is 1.72x (2.41x) faster than KLU and 1.46x (1.98x) faster than one-thread CKTSO. Built with gcc 4.8.5 and nvcc 11.0 on CentOS 7.9; flags are not stated, there is no benchmark code, and per-matrix results appear only as bar charts.
status_note: Abandoned since 2023-04-01 (22 commits, 6 stars), binary-only with no license terms, so reference only; tied to CUDA 11.0-era builds and an external licensed CKTSO library.
